stem: A shoot tip lit from one side bends towards the light because auxin
options: accumulates on the shaded side and makes those cells elongate more
is destroyed on the shaded side, so cells on the lit side grow faster
moves to the lit side and makes those cells divide
stops all growth on the lit side by closing stomata
explanation: Auxin moves away from light, so the shaded side gets more of it; its cells elongate faster and the shoot curves towards the light (positive phototropism). Auxin promotes cell elongation in shoots, not closing of stomata, which is the role of abscisic acid.

stem: The plant hormone that causes rapid stem elongation (bolting) and helps break seed dormancy in cereals is
explanation: Gibberellins promote internode elongation and, in germinating cereal grains, trigger amylase production that mobilises stored starch. Abscisic acid has the opposite effect, maintaining dormancy.

stem: During drought, the hormone that causes stomata to close and reduces water loss is
explanation: Water stress raises abscisic acid levels in leaves; it makes guard cells lose K⁺ and water, so the stomata close. It is called the stress hormone, while cytokinins delay ageing and promote cell division.

stem: The gaseous plant hormone that speeds up the ripening of fruits such as bananas and mangoes is
explanation: Ethylene (ethene) is a gas released by ripening fruit, which is why one ripe fruit hastens the ripening of others stored with it. Auxin and gibberellin mainly control growth.

stem: Nerve impulses travel faster along myelinated neurons because
options: myelin itself carries the electric current along the axon
the impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next
myelinated axons have no sodium channels at all
the axon is thinner under the myelin sheath
explanation: Myelin made by Schwann cells insulates the axon, so depolarisation occurs only at the gaps (nodes of Ranvier) and the impulse leaps between them (saltatory conduction). Myelin is an insulator and does not conduct the current itself.

stem: The sodium-potassium pump helps maintain the resting potential of a neuron by moving, for each ATP used,
options: 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ into it
2 Na⁺ out of the cell and 3 K⁺ into it
3 Na⁺ into the cell and 2 K⁺ out of it
equal numbers of Na⁺ and K⁺ in both directions
explanation: The pump expels three sodium ions and brings in two potassium ions per cycle, so more positive charge leaves than enters, helping keep the inside negative at about −70 mV. Swapping the numbers would make the inside more positive.

stem: The rising phase (depolarisation) of an action potential is caused by
options: rapid outflow of K⁺ ions from the axon
inflow of Cl⁻ ions into the axon
rapid inflow of Na⁺ ions into the axon
the sodium-potassium pump working faster than usual
explanation: A stimulus opens voltage-gated sodium channels, and Na⁺ rushes in, reversing the potential to about +40 mV. The outflow of K⁺ comes next and causes repolarisation.

stem: At a chemical synapse, an impulse can pass in only one direction because
options: the synaptic cleft allows ions to flow only one way
the postsynaptic neuron has no sodium channels
acetylcholine is destroyed in the presynaptic knob
only the presynaptic knob releases neurotransmitter and only the postsynaptic membrane has its receptors
explanation: Vesicles of neurotransmitter such as acetylcholine are found only in the presynaptic terminal, and the receptors for it are on the postsynaptic membrane, so transmission is one-way. Acetylcholine is broken down by acetylcholinesterase in the cleft, not in the knob.

stem: In a reflex arc, the neuron that carries impulses from the spinal cord to the effector muscle is the
explanation: The path is receptor, sensory neuron, relay neuron in the spinal cord, motor neuron, effector. Sensory neurons carry impulses towards the spinal cord, not away from it.

stem: Maintaining balance and coordinating smooth, precise movements is the main function of the
explanation: The cerebellum receives information from muscles, joints and the inner ear and fine-tunes movements. The cerebrum starts voluntary movements and the medulla controls breathing and heart rate.

stem: The part of the brain that controls breathing rate, heart rate and blood pressure is the
explanation: The medulla in the hindbrain contains the cardiovascular and respiratory centres, which work without conscious control. Damage there is often fatal, while the cerebellum controls balance.

stem: Insulin, which lowers blood glucose level, is secreted by the
options: α-cells of the islets of Langerhans
β-cells of the islets of Langerhans
explanation: Insulin from β-cells makes liver and muscle cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen. α-cells secrete glucagon, which raises blood glucose, so the two cell types are easily swapped.

stem: A lack of iodine in the diet often leads to an enlarged thyroid gland (goitre) because iodine is needed to make
explanation: Thyroxine contains iodine; when it cannot be made, low thyroxine allows high TSH from the pituitary, which keeps stimulating the thyroid to enlarge. Insulin, adrenaline and growth hormone contain no iodine.

stem: When the level of thyroxine in the blood rises above normal, the secretion of TSH by the anterior pituitary
options: increases, an example of positive feedback
decreases, an example of positive feedback
stays the same, as the two are unrelated
decreases, an example of negative feedback
explanation: High thyroxine inhibits the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, so less TSH is released and thyroxine output falls back to normal. Feedback that reverses the change is negative; positive feedback would push the level even higher.

stem: Newly hatched ducklings follow the first moving object they see, even a human, and keep following it. This behaviour is called
explanation: Imprinting is rapid learning during a short sensitive period early in life, studied by Konrad Lorenz with geese. Habituation is learning to ignore a repeated harmless stimulus, which does not fit this case.
